plan.title: Asakusa: Old Tokyo on foot
plan.summary: Through the Thunder Gate to Tokyo's oldest temple and the shrine that survived the war, then out along an Edo-style street to the Sumida river, where the old city meets the Skytree.

stops.name: Kaminarimon
stops.angle: The Thunder Gate: a 700-kilo lantern, two gods of wind and thunder, and a gate paid for by an electronics company.
stops.walkingCueToHere: Stand in front of the gate, under the big red lantern.
stops.script: Welcome to Asakusa, and to the Kaminarimon, the Thunder Gate. Look up at the lantern first. It is red paper and bamboo, nearly four metres tall, and it weighs around seven hundred kilos. The characters on it read 'Kaminarimon', and if you walk underneath and look up, there is a carved dragon on its base. On either side of you stand two guardians: Fūjin, the god of wind, carrying his bag of storms, and Raijin, the god of thunder, ringed by drums. They are here to keep bad weather and bad luck out of the temple grounds, which is a sensible job for a gate in a city of wooden buildings. It did not always work. A gate has stood here, in one form or another, for about a thousand years, and it has burned down more than once. The last time was in 1865, and for almost a century there was no gate at all. The one you are looking at went up in 1960, paid for by Kōnosuke Matsushita, the founder of the company we now call Panasonic, who had been cured of an illness after praying here. Look at the bottom of the lantern and you will find his company's name. So the most photographed gate in Tokyo is, among other things, a thank-you note from an electronics company. Walk through it now, and keep going straight: the street on the other side has been selling things to pilgrims for three hundred years.

stops.name: Nakamise-dōri
stops.angle: One of Japan's oldest shopping streets, started when locals were allowed to sell in return for sweeping the temple grounds.
stops.walkingCueToHere: Walk straight through the gate and into the long street of small shops.
stops.script: This is Nakamise-dōri, the street of the inner shops. It runs about two hundred and fifty metres from the Thunder Gate to the next gate, and there are close to ninety shops along it. It is one of the oldest shopping streets in Japan, and it began with a deal. Around the beginning of the eighteenth century, the people who lived next to the temple were given permission to set up stalls along the approach, and in return they were expected to keep the grounds clean. Sweep the path, and you may sell on it. That arrangement became this. Look at what is on sale and you can still see who the customers were meant to be: pilgrims and day-trippers. Rice crackers, sweet bean cakes, folding fans, wooden combs, little charms. Watch for the shops making ningyō-yaki, small cakes baked in iron moulds, filled with red bean paste, some of them shaped like the lantern you just walked under. The buildings themselves are not old. The city rebuilt the street in brick in 1885, it was damaged in the earthquake of 1923, and it was bombed in 1945, so what you see is a post-war rebuild. But the shape of it, a narrow straight line of stalls leading the eye to the temple, is the same one a visitor from Edo would recognise. One local rule worth knowing: it is considered bad manners to eat while walking here. Stand by the shop, finish, then carry on to the gate at the end.

stops.name: Sensō-ji
stops.angle: Tokyo's oldest temple, founded for a statue two fishermen pulled out of the river, and never shown to anyone since.
stops.walkingCueToHere: Go through the Hōzōmon gate with the giant straw sandals and walk up to the main hall.
stops.script: You are at Sensō-ji, the oldest temple in Tokyo. As you came through the Hōzōmon, the gate with the enormous straw sandals hanging on its back, you passed under a promise: those sandals are woven in a village in Yamagata and brought here, and they are meant to tell any demons that a giant guards this place. The story of the temple begins in the year 628, in the river you will see at the end of this walk. Two brothers, Hinokuma Hamanari and Hinokuma Takenari, were fishing in the Sumida when they found a small golden statue of Kannon, the bodhisattva of mercy, in their net. They threw it back. It came back. The village headman, Haji no Nakatomo, recognised what it was, made his own house into a temple for it, and spent the rest of his life there. That statue is still said to be inside the main hall in front of you, and nobody sees it. It is a hidden image, kept out of sight, and that has been the rule for centuries. Before you go up the steps, look for the large bronze incense burner. People waft the smoke over themselves, onto the head for wisdom, onto a sore shoulder or knee to heal it. The hall itself is a rebuild: the original was destroyed in the American air raid of March 1945, which burned much of this part of the city, and this one was finished in 1958 in concrete. If you want your fortune, the omikuji drawers are to the sides. A bad fortune is tied to the racks and left behind.

stops.name: Asakusa Shrine
stops.angle: A Shinto shrine to the three men who found the statue, built by a shōgun in 1649 and one of the few things here the war left standing.
stops.walkingCueToHere: From the main hall, walk to the right, past the side of the building, to the smaller shrine behind it.
stops.script: Step away from the crowds for a moment. This quieter building is Asakusa Shrine, and it belongs to the same story as the temple next door. It is a Shinto shrine, and the gods it honours are the three men from the river: the two fishing brothers, and Haji no Nakatomo, the headman who built the first temple. In Japan a Buddhist temple and a Shinto shrine standing side by side is completely ordinary, and for most of history the two were run together. This building was put up in 1649 on the orders of the shōgun Tokugawa Iemitsu, and here is the remarkable thing: it survived. The earthquake of 1923 and the fire-bombing of 1945 destroyed almost everything around you, but this shrine came through both, and it is now an Important Cultural Property. Look at the details, the lacquer, the carved and painted panels under the roof, and you are looking at the real seventeenth century, not a copy. In May this is the centre of the Sanja Matsuri, the festival of the three shrines, one of the wildest in Tokyo. Over a weekend, portable shrines are carried through the streets of Asakusa on the shoulders of shouting crowds, bounced and shaken to make the gods inside more powerful. If you would like to pray, the routine is simple: a coin in the box, bow twice, clap twice, a moment of thought, and one more bow.

stops.name: Denbōin-dōri
stops.angle: An old-Edo shopping street with a famous thief on the roof.
stops.walkingCueToHere: Head back down towards Nakamise and turn right into the wide street with dark wooden shopfronts.
stops.script: This is Denbōin-dōri, named after the Denbō-in, the residence of the temple's head priests, whose garden sits behind the walls on your right. The street was remade to look like the Edo period, the centuries before 1868 when Tokyo was still called Edo and was run by the shōguns. Dark wood, tiled roofs, painted signboards: it is a stage set, but a good one, and the shops behind it are real, selling everything from wooden geta sandals to tenugui, the printed cotton cloths that people here use as towels, wrapping and headbands. Now look up at the rooftops, because this street keeps its stories above eye level. Somewhere along here you will find a little figure of a man crouching on the roof, a cloth tied over his face. That is Nezumi Kozō, the rat boy, the most famous thief of Edo. In the early nineteenth century he broke into the mansions of samurai lords, again and again, and the legend grew that he gave what he stole to the poor. The real Jirokichi probably spent it on gambling, and he was executed in 1832, but the city preferred the legend. A thief who robbed only the powerful made a good hero for the ordinary people of Edo, who lived, worked and shopped on streets exactly like this one. Carry on east now, back across the main road, towards the river.

stops.name: Azuma Bridge
stops.angle: The red bridge over the Sumida, with the city's newest tower and its strangest building in one view.
stops.walkingCueToHere: Walk east to the river and out onto the red bridge.
stops.script: This is the Sumida river, and the red bridge under you is Azumabashi. There has been a bridge here since 1774, when it was one of only a handful across the Sumida, and it was built with tolls to pay for it. Look along the water: this is the river where, according to the temple, the two brothers found their statue nearly fourteen hundred years ago. In the Edo period it was the city's playground, lined with teahouses, crowded with pleasure boats in summer, lit by fireworks. That last tradition survived: on one night in late July, the Sumida River Fireworks fill this whole sky. Now look across. The tall white tower is the Tokyo Skytree, finished in 2012, six hundred and thirty-four metres tall, a number chosen because it can be read as 'Musashi', the old name for this region. And the black building beside it, with the strange golden shape on its roof, is the Asahi Beer Hall, designed by Philippe Starck in 1989. The shape is meant to be a flame, the burning heart of Asahi beer. Nobody in Tokyo calls it that. They call it the golden turd. So there you have it, in one view: a river from a seventh-century miracle, a bridge from the age of the shōguns, and the twenty-first century on the far bank. That is the end of the walk. Thank you for coming along through old Asakusa.
